L7: ## What we do
L8: 
L9: CASTR Alliance aims to advance human and veterinary medicine by facilitating the discovery of innovative treatments through the management of high-quality veterinary clinical studies and collaboration with industry leaders and veterinary hospitals.
L10: 
L11: We provide turnkey management of sponsored veterinary clinical studies to pharmaceutical and medical device development teams worldwide.
L12: We partner with state-of-the-art veterinary specialty and referral hospitals throughout the Pacific Northwest and beyond to enroll patients on sponsored clinical studies.
L13: 
L14: We manage sponsored clinical trials that abide by Good Clinical Practice (GCP) standards for veterinary studies and are designed to ensure the collection of high-quality data.
L15: We submit all CASTR-run studies for ethical review by an external Veterinary Clinical Studies Committee (VCSC) to prioritize the safety and well-being of all patients.
L16: 
L17: 【4†MORE DETAILS】
L18: ## What motivates us
L19: 
L20: The motivations behind CASTR Alliance’s efforts are to connect companion animals with cutting-edge treatments, address naturally occurring diseases in pets, and accelerate medical innovation for both animals and humans through clinical trials.
L21: 
L22: #### Linking Patients to Caregivers
L23: 
L24: Our sponsored studies link companion animals in need of innovative solutions to novel therapeutic or diagnostic options that may otherwise be unavailable to them.
L25: #### Studying Spontaneous Diseases
L26: 
L27: Our research focuses on spontaneous diseases – those that arise naturally in dogs and cats. By enrolling companion animals who are already afflicted or symptomatic, we aim to provide potential direct benefits to our pets while gathering data that could help human or animal patients in the future.
L28: 
L29: #### Accelerating Medical Innovation
L30: 
L31: When a pet is enrolled in a CASTR-managed clinical trial, they take part in helping advance medical discovery and innovation.
L32: ## 【5†Translational research:】 Caring for our pets while advancing human and animal healthcare
L33: 
L34: ## What to expect
L35: 
L36: #### Contracting companies
L37: 
L38: can expect all CASTR Alliance-run studies to be managed efficiently and ethically, adhere to GCP standards, and result in high quality data. We deliver progress updates upon request throughout the trial, conduct diligent site and safety monitoring, and provide data at interim analysis, and at the conclusion of the trial.
L39: #### Veterinary clinicians
L40: 
L41: and support staff participating in the study are trained from the onset on the trial protocol to ensure treatment is conducted according to our rigorous standards. We continue to provide guidance and support to our participating sites throughout the entire course of the study.
L42: #### Pet owners
L43: 
L44: who enroll their pets in these clinical studies engage directly with a participating veterinary center, where all study procedures are carried out in accordance with the established study protocol. Studies are typically supported such that treatment is partially or fully covered by the sponsor.
L45: ## WHO WE ARE
L46: CASTR Alliance was founded in 2019 by veterinary clinician-scientists Jessica Bertout and Jim Perry. As scientists, they bring extensive experience in designing, managing, and conducting clinical trials that meet the rigorous standards of the biotech industry. Moreover, as devoted pet owners and veterinarians, they are personally committed to delivering the highest quality care for our animal companions. Together, Drs.
L47: Bertout and Perry created CASTR Alliance to leverage their expertise and advance medicine for humans and animals alike.

L69: DCM in Dobermans
L70: Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a disease of heart muscle that results in a decreased ability of the heart to pump blood. The prognosis for DCM is often poor, with a less than 50% survival rate one year after clinical signs develop, unless a reversible underlying cause is identified. There is no available cure for Dilated Cardiomyopathy, current techniques focus on extending survival time as long as possible.
L71: However the focus of this clinical trial is to evaluate a potential curative treatment for cardiomyopathy in the Doberman Pinscher.

L82:

L85: Selective Inhibition of Nuclear Export (SINE) and Canine Osteosarcoma
L86: Osteosarcoma is a common cancer diagnosed in dogs, particularly in large breed dogs. While several chemotherapy protocols have been shown to provide modest management of the onset of metastasis (spread of cancer), we are continuously looking for additional treatments that may extend survival time. Carboplatin is a widely accepted chemotherapy agent used in treatment of osteosarcoma.
L87: The results of this study will allow us to determine if dogs can successfully tolerate carboplatin and a new drug called Laverdia-CA1 (verdinexor) in a combination protocol.

L98:

L101: Performance of a New Point-of-care Rapid Test to Diagnose Pulmonary Coccidioidomycosis
L102: Diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis in dogs is challenging due to the fact that the symptoms are not specific for this disease. Coccidioidomycosis can be diagnosed via a biopsy however the most common method is testing for antibodies to the fungus. These tests are often sent to third party labs delaying confirmation of the disease.
L103: This study looks to evaluate a potential point of care rapid test which would be able to provide a positive or negative result indicating the presence or absence of antibodies, respectively, within 30-60 minutes. The diagnosis of pulmonary coccidioidomycosis can be difficult because clinical signs overlap with many other respiratory tract disorders and dogs can have positive Valley Fever antibody titers without active clinical infection.
L104: Acute phase proteins are useful biomarkers for many other disorders and our hope is to determine whether they can facilitate making a diagnosis of pulmonary coccidioidomycosis in dogs. For additional details or questions please contact Dr. Jaffey (jjaffe@midwestern.edu).

L115: Efficacy of twice-daily nebulized budesonide for the treatment of canine chronic bronchitis and eosinophilic lung disease
L116: 
L117: Interventional
L118: 
L119: Efficacy of twice-daily nebulized budesonide for the treatment of canine chronic bronchitis and eosinophilic lung disease
L120: Canine chronic bronchitis and eosinophilic lung disease are inflammatory diseases characterized by cough for > 2 months without another identifiable cause. Dogs with chronic bronchitis have persistent airway neutrophilic inflammation. The foundation of long-term therapy is corticosteroids. Oral prednisone is commonly used but has a litany of possible adverse effects. Inhaled steroids is an alternative to avoid the adverse effects of prednisone but the only available option is fluticasone.
L121: This medication is expensive and has variable efficacy. Inhaled budesonide is a medication used in humans to treat a similar airway disorder and is a fraction of the cost. This study aims to investigate the benefit of inhaled budesonide on respiratory tract symptoms in dogs with inflammatory airway disorders.
